title: A Desperate Prayer From the Ruins
overview: With their city and temple destroyed, the people beg God to break into the world as he once did, confessing their failures while appealing to him as their Father.

parts.label: Tear open the sky (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: The speakers ask God to rip open the heavens and come down with fire-like power, recalling past moments when he did 'awesome things' no one expected. The text names no event; it is most often read as the shaking of Mount Sinai, though some have suggested other rescues, and Christians later read verse 4 through Paul, who quotes it about what God has prepared for those who love him.

parts.label: An honest confession (vv. 5-7)
parts.note: God helps those who gladly do right, but the speakers admit they kept failing, and the middle of verse 5 is hard to read in Hebrew, so translations differ. They say even their good deeds are like a cloth stained with menstrual blood, which made a person ritually unclean under their law, and they picture themselves as dry leaves blown away, with no one even praying anymore.

parts.label: Father and potter (vv. 8-9)
parts.note: The prayer turns on the word 'yet': God is still their Father, and they are clay he shaped with his own hands. On the strength of that bond, they ask him not to stay angry forever.

parts.label: A city in ashes (vv. 10-12)
parts.note: Jerusalem lies empty and the temple where their ancestors worshiped has been burned, which most scholars connect to the Babylonian destruction of 586 BC. The prayer ends on an open question, asking whether God will stay silent after all this.

think: Can a person admit their own part in a disaster and still honestly ask why help has not come, or do those two feelings pull against each other?
